title: What will next gen games look like with Ai raising the bar?
author: ComprehensiveBox2357
selftext:
Many are producing slop yes. But AI can also empower amazing creatives and devs to create even better games. 

Realistic graphics (DLSS) will probably get old quick, but I’m just wondering if there’s another level besides idk GTA VI.

comments.author: Fancy-Plenty6712
comments.body: I'd like to think NPC's are going to become a whole lot better. I'd also say that it should likely allow map sizes on games to become way bigger too. Thing like the actual game engines themselves probably will get a level up but the most noticeable stuff will be how much bigger games will feel. I hope.

replies.author: potentially__potent
replies.body: On your game engine point - I think AI is going to fix the unoptimised mess that companies have been putting out. More optimised engines will improve performance and allow more gameplay mechanics to fit in.

replies.author: GlobalCurry
replies.body: I think with the hardware shortages for the foreseeable future there will be an ongoing push for optimization too.

replies.author: potentially__potent
replies.body: Totally agree, I think that comes from the pressure to deliver in the industry as well as laziness. Love or hate AI, it's going to improve a lot of things for gaming and beyond.

replies.author: ComprehensiveBox2357
replies.body: I think you’re on to something with the NPC’s. Maybe there will be games that pair you up with an AI that plays with you like a human would.

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
We're likely due for static dialogue trees for a long time still because running an LLM locally requires a lot of resources and running one remotely implies huge cost. 

However, huge dialogue trees with baked TTS (many hundreds of thousands of lines) is super possible.

replies.author: ComprehensiveBox2357
replies.body: Yeah fake inference can still be achieved with enough tokens haha

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
Always difficult to try and predict the future, but I'd be shocked if NVidia's new generative texture technology isn't a big part it.

I know everyone loves to have the DLSS trailer for Resident Evil because they don't feel that the way Grace was rendered matched the version of Grace in their head, and that's fine... but look at the quality of the materials and the environment in that trailer. It's completely insane, IMHO. And if the character hadn't been Grace, and people didn't know it was AI technology, everyone would have been completely blown away.

It's just a night and day difference in fidelity.

If I were to make a bet on something, it's that someone will use either that technology or a sister technology to it that doesn't have the marketing baggage to make a good game, their game will look completely incredible, and that will cause a huge cultural schism. Anti-AI people will insist the game be boycotted or whatever and post disingenuous clickbait videos where they zoom in on whatever imperfections... everyone else will play the game, get used to that level of fidelity, and not want to go back to lower quality materials and textures.

  
There's also a very real possibility that the American / western market will learn the hard way that this technology is the future. China, Korea and Japan seem to have to qualms with it at all (...which is kind of wild to me, because Japan by tradition has been extremely slow to adopt new technology post-2000s), which means their firms will benefit from it and if western studios do not... they'll get pushed out of the market. It'll be like car manufacturing all over again, where resistance to change with the time resulted in American manufacturers being unable to compete against German and Japanese competitors, and then those manufacturers went through incredibly brutal contractions (the damage done from that is still felt in parts of America to this day).

comments.author: TechgeekOne
comments.body:
I'm personally looking forward to a lot of things. But I've also seen/made the sausage so I'm biased lol.
- NPC behaviors could be more varied and contextual. One of the limiting factors is writing all the states, transitions, and getting them to make sense in the game world. Even with more advanced planners like an HTN or behavior tree it's still a grind to setup and at some point you have to draw a line or you'll never be done. There's also the potential for small fine tuned models to act out a character on the fly and build the responses from a generic set of poses and a big dialog bank. Probably not free-form text gen though because that has the jailbreak problem.
- Detail in the worlds, like clutter or easter eggs. One major limiting factor in how sparse or densely populated a game world is with clutter is the time to create the assets and place everything. Proc-gen can solve some of that but having AI available to create the generator or place itself will help a ton.
- More varied content. Part of the problem with open world games is they start to feel samey because someone/thing has to fill the world with locations, quests, points of interest, characters, etc. Those all take time to create, place, test, and at some point you have to cut corners or the game would never be finished. AI removes most of that grunt work from the equation letting you be really creative without the scope exceeding your budget.
- Better animation and motion. Even with modern techniques like motion matching there's still limitations to the animation quality and number of poses you can get from raw mocap of actors, and it's usually not dynamic with the environment so you still get weird blends or bad alignment (foot sliding, missed chairs/levers/doors, etc). The stuff I've been seeing coming out of the pose generation corner of ML has been really interesting and I really look forward to the day it makes it into games.
- Less bugs and better perf. From personal experience it's a _constant_ battle to get time to spend on performance or bug fixing, and even if you do it's pulling teeth to get anyone outside of a small group in the studio to care or stop making messes long enough that you can make progress. AI makes half that go away because it can do the testing en masse for cheap and it can do the long and "unproductive" profiling and refactoring work to improve performance.
- This seems like a weird one, but better game design. One of the bottlenecks during pre-production is that your engineering team can only prototype so many mechanics before you run out of time, and they can only turn so many of them into production mechanics before you have to start cutting things to hit the release date. AI cuts that cost to next to nothing, meaning you can just try out wild ideas and see if they're fun. If they are building everything out into a solid design or making changes late in development is perfectly viable, meaning you get a better game on the end.
- There's a whole magical world of unexplored potential in integrating LLMs, CNNs, and the myriad of other kinds of neural networks into games for various purposes. Idk what could be here but it's definitely something I want to explore eventually.

comments.author: FlightFit335
comments.body: Manufacturing will balance out in the next coming years as plants cone online.  This will allow for GPUs with greater memory.  Point being a game will load a 2B parameter model that will be able do NPC dialogue.  No 2 players will experience the same commentary.
